FINDING_ID: LB_F001  
SEVERITY: 0.84  
FLAW_CLASS: 1  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.78  
DESCRIPTION: `DynamicManager.process_round()` reassigns roles before it updates `self._live_fingerprints`. That means the role map used for the next round is based on fingerprints through round `r-1`, not the performance just observed in round `r`. I verified this with a small repro: after round 0, `m3` became the strongest live COL candidate, but `role_map` still kept `m2` as COL until a second manual `reassign()` call. This makes PM/COL/PAR admissibility lag one round behind observed performance.  
PROPOSED_FIX: In `process_round()`, call `update_fingerprints(round_idx, findings, responses)` before `role_assignment.reassign(...)`, still before appending the new `RoundResult`. Then sync `failure_handler.role_map` from the freshly reassigned roles.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_F002  
SEVERITY: 0.80  
FLAW_CLASS: 1  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.84  
DESCRIPTION: The adaptive coverage metric `C` is structurally biased by allocation. `update_fingerprints()` computes `C` as `distinct flaw classes found by this model / total flaw classes found by anyone this round`. So a model’s “coverage breadth” depends on what other models happened to find and on how narrowly it was tasked, not on its own opportunity set. That creates a self-reinforcing routing bias: a model assigned only one flaw class can never earn a high `C` in a diverse round, so later role/capability decisions keep treating it as narrow even if it perfectly covered everything it was asked to review. The root ownership problem is visible in the same path: `process_round()` ignores its `tasks` argument and stores `RoundResult.allocation=None`, so the manager has no per-model opportunity data when updating fingerprints.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Persist the actual round allocation into `RoundResult` and pass it into `update_fingerprints()`. Compute coverage against the flaw classes assigned to that model, or against a stable global class universe, rather than the peer round-union denominator.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_F003  
SEVERITY: 0.78  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.73  
DESCRIPTION: Upstream of the shown slice, the dispatch false-positive learning loop is unwired. `DetectorHealthMonitor.check_dispatch_health()` expects `dispatch_successes_after_block`, and `DynamicManager` defines `record_dispatch_success_after_block()`, but there are no call sites anywhere in the repo. So a model can be blocked, later succeed via decomposition, and the immune layer will never receive the success signal needed to diagnose a false-positive block or add that model to `pre_decompose_models`. The “learn from blocked-then-succeeded dispatches” path is therefore dead code.  
PROPOSED_FIX: In the dispatch/orchestration path, when a model that was previously blocked is successfully run after decomposition, call `mgr.record_dispatch_success_after_block(model_id, round_idx)` and add a regression test that proves `check_dispatch_health()` can now emit the dispatch false-positive diagnosis.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_F004  
SEVERITY: 0.82  
FLAW_CLASS: 5  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.69  
DESCRIPTION: Upstream of the shown slice, the probabilistic feasibility gate is not actually enforced on the fallback path. In `run_exp17_immune._dispatch_round()` and the analogous path in `run_exp12_live_wire.py`, when `mgr.check_dispatch_feasibility()` blocks a prompt, the code auto-builds a decomposed prompt but never re-runs the feasibility check on that new prompt before dispatching it. So a still-too-large decomposed prompt is sent unchecked, which defeats the whole capacity-protection mechanism precisely when it is most needed.  
PROPOSED_FIX: After building the decomposed or sub-area prompt, recompute the token estimate and call `check_dispatch_feasibility()` again. If it still fails, do not dispatch; escalate to a smaller decomposition level or skip that model for the round.  
VERIFIED: TRUE
